L8-a8d545: **Blind (non-visual) internal-urethrotomy instrument** that combines calibrated dilation with a controlled longitudinal cold-knife incision at the 12 o'clock dorsal midline as the device is withdrawn. The historical predecessor to direct-vision internal urethrotomy (DVIU); now largely supplanted by the Sachse direct-vision urethrotome but retaining a niche role in meatal or fossa-navicularis stricture and in resource-limited settings. Named for Fessenden Nott Otis (1825–1900), the American urologist who is also the namesake of the [Otis Bougie-à-Boule](/docs/foundations/tools/instruments/sounds-bougies/otis-bougie). The ICS male LUTS-surgery terminology document explicitly defines blind urethrotomy as "opening of the stricture with the use of a special instrument (Otis urethrotome) to perform the incision without direct visualization."<sup>[[1]](#ref1)</sup>
L13-d78d40: - **Calibrated expandable distal segment.** Turning a screw on the handle widens the segment to a precise French diameter shown on a graduated handle scale, allowing measured dilation before the cut.
L14-2cdc23: - **Concealed retractable cold-knife blade** housed within the shaft; when deployed, the blade extends from a longitudinal slot and cuts at the 12 o'clock position as the instrument is withdrawn.
L18-431347: The two functions in one instrument, dilating and then incising on withdrawal, distinguish the Otis from both a plain sound (no cut) and the Sachse or Collins-knife systems (cut under vision, no calibrated dilation).
L24-bd8aad: - **Meatal and fossa-navicularis strictures.** The short straight distal urethra is the safest anatomy for a blind dorsal-midline cut; the Otis retains a small role here when DVIU equipment is not at hand.
L25-5af05b: - **Resource-limited settings.** The Otis is used when an endoscopic urethrotome and irrigation system are unavailable.
L26-d661e4: - **Bulbar strictures.** These were historically managed with the Otis; modern practice uses [DVIU](/docs/surgical-techniques/04a-urethral-reconstruction/dviu) instead.
L30-4cf328: The Otis was widely used as a preliminary cut at the meatus and distal urethra before TURP to accommodate the 24–28 Fr resectoscope sheath and reduce post-TURP stricture rates.
L32-1023c8: - **Schultz 1989 RCT (n = 185).** Otis urethrotomy before TURP gave a 4% stricture rate versus 16% with catheter dilation (significant).<sup>[[5]](#ref5)</sup>
L33-aac2d2: - **Nielsen 1989 RCT (n = 200).** No significant difference: urethrotomy and TURP 14% versus TURP alone 21%; the authors concluded that "urethrotomy before TURP cannot prevent postoperative urethral strictures."<sup>[[6]](#ref6)</sup>
L34-79769e: - The practice has largely fallen out of favor with smaller-caliber endoscopic platforms (HoLEP, ThuLEP, bipolar enucleation) that do not require a 28-Fr sheath.<sup>[[7]](#ref7)</sup>
L36-fa5571: For procedural context, see [DVIU and Urethral Dilation](/docs/surgical-techniques/04a-urethral-reconstruction/dviu).
L40-de312f: 1. **General or regional anesthesia.** The blind dilation component is more painful than a visual urethrotomy under local.<sup>[[3]](#ref3)</sup>
L42-af1819: 3. **Advancement past the stricture.** If the stricture is too tight, preliminary [filiform-and-follower](/docs/foundations/tools/instruments/sounds-bougies/filiforms-followers) or sound dilation is used.
L43-ca659b: 4. **Expansion.** Turn the screw to widen the segment to the target caliber (approximately 28–30 Fr in the adult male).
L44-169578: 5. **Blade deployment and slow withdrawal.** The blade makes a clean dorsal-midline longitudinal cut as the expanded segment is pulled back through the stricture.
L62-4a150e: - **Frohmüller / Bülow 1975.** Otis urethrotomy in 23 patients; approximately 60% required no further dilations; low complication rate.<sup>[[2]](#ref2)</sup>
L63-1059dd: - **Hjortrup 1983.** 72 consecutive patients over 5 years; success 82% (95% CI 71–90%) at mean 29-month follow-up.<sup>[[3]](#ref3)</sup>
L64-fb9d31: - **Cochrane (Wong 2012).** The only RCT directly comparing dilation to urethrotomy used the Sachse technique, not the Otis; head-to-head data between Otis and Sachse remain sparse.<sup>[[4]](#ref4)</sup>
L65-68c639: - **AUA 2023.** Dilation and DVIU are interchangeable first-line options for short bulbar strictures, with the highest success rates in bulbar strictures < 1 cm; success falls rapidly with length, recurrence, penile location, and ischemic etiology.<sup>[[8]](#ref8)</sup>
L66-1aec5a: - **Verla 2019 review.** DVIU success up to approximately 80% for primary strictures < 2 cm; figures likely transfer roughly to Otis urethrotomy in equivalent anatomy.<sup>[[9]](#ref9)</sup>
L70-fb7981: - **False passage.** The principal complication of the blind technique and the rationale for the modern shift to DVIU.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[3]](#ref3)</sup>
L71-bc7b98: - **Uncontrolled incision depth.** The 12 o'clock cut goes through whatever tissue is at the blade; in pendulous urethra this risks corporal-tunica injury.
L72-443fa1: - **Urethral hemorrhage, UTI, bacteremia.** These are standard urethral-instrumentation risks.
L73-d849c5: - **Stricture recurrence.** The underlying biology (re-fibrosis) is unchanged by switching from blind to visual incision; recurrence remains the principal limitation of any endoscopic stricture management.
L77-93f3cc: The Otis has been supplanted by the Sachse DVIU for the great majority of indications because:<sup>[[3]](#ref3)[[4]](#ref4)</sup>
L81-912f03: - **Office / local-anesthesia DVIU** is possible in selected cases.
L82-51e922: - The Otis remains useful for meatal or fossa-navicularis strictures and in equipment-limited settings.
L86-0553fd: The Otis urethrotome was one of the first instruments to move stricture management beyond simple dilation toward controlled incision. Otis's principle that a measured, calibrated longitudinal cut heals across to a wider lumen rather than tearing scar is the conceptual ancestor of modern DVIU and remains the foundation of endoscopic stricture management today.<sup>[[9]](#ref9)</sup>
